findings.issue: POST /api/onboarding/step/9 (step9_consent) is reachable by any authenticated user at any time - it does not check onboarding_step or onboarding_complete - and calls record_consent(), which appends a new row with event defaulting to 'granted' and the flags taken from the request body. Because current_consent()/consent_allows() read the latest row, replaying step 9 after a withdrawal silently re-grants auto_apply and llm_processing and re-enables the gates added in app/tasks/auto_apply.py. Withdrawing data_processing deactivates the user so that path self-closes, but auto_apply-only and llm_processing-only withdrawals are fully reversible through this untouched endpoint, with no 'regrant after withdrawal' audit event. The story lists re-grant as out of scope, but the bypass itself is unguarded. Not a BLOCK: the only actor is the user's own session (SameSite=lax + origin-restricted CORS rule out a cross-site trigger).
findings.fix: Reject step 9 when user.onboarding_complete is true (409), or route re-grant through an explicit endpoint that writes event='granted' after a withdrawal and audits 'consent.regranted' with the scopes.

findings.issue: apply_matched_jobs reads the consent record once, before the tenant loop, and reuses that snapshot for the whole run (auto_apply gate at line 82, llm_processing gate at line 96). A withdrawal committed after the snapshot does not stop the in-flight run, which can keep tailoring resumes, calling the LLM provider and submitting portal applications up to the daily cap. DPDP Act s.6(4) requires processing under withdrawn consent to stop; enforcement here is only effective from the next task run.
findings.fix: Re-read consent (or re-check consent_allows against a freshly loaded record) inside the per-job loop before each LLM call and before each apply_to_job, and abort the loop when the scope is no longer allowed.

findings.issue: Withdrawing data_processing is enforced only indirectly: consent_store.withdraw_consent commits the consent row first, then execute_deletion(soft_delete) separately sets users.is_active=False, and it is that flag - not a consent check - that stops match_jobs.py:123, ml_retrain.py:117 and status_check.py:46 from processing the user's data. The two commits are not atomic, so if disable_auto_apply or execute_deletion raises (tenant schema unavailable, DB error), the request returns 500 with consent already withdrawn while those tasks keep processing the user. No processing path other than auto_apply consults consent_allows(record, 'data_processing').
findings.fix: Add an explicit consent_allows(..., 'data_processing') check at the head of match_jobs, ml_retrain and status_check per-user work, and/or make withdrawal + side effects one transaction (or a retried outbox) so a partial failure cannot leave processing enabled after a recorded withdrawal.

findings.issue: The raw User-Agent header is passed through unbounded to ConsentRecord.user_agent, which is String(512) (app/compliance/dpdpa.py:25). A request with a longer UA makes the INSERT fail on PostgreSQL; the DataError propagates to the global handler in app/main.py, which logs error=str(exc) plus the stack trace at ERROR level - and the SQLAlchemy exception string carries the bound parameters, i.e. the ip_address and user_agent, because the engine in app/database.py is created without hide_parameters=True. So a client-controlled input both breaks a compliance action (500 instead of a recorded withdrawal) and puts the IP/UA into the log stream that AC4 deliberately keeps them out of. Same untruncated pattern exists in record_consent (pre-existing).
findings.fix: Truncate/validate in the router or in _withdrawal_row (user_agent[:512], ip_address[:45]) before constructing the row, and set hide_parameters=True on the engine (or scrub parameters in the global exception handler).

findings.issue: 'Current consent' is defined by ORDER BY consented_at with no tiebreaker, and it is implemented twice: DESC LIMIT 1 here and history[-1] in app/routers/consent.py:33. consented_at is generated in Python (datetime.now), so a grant and a withdrawal written in the same microsecond, or a clock step on a multi-instance deployment, makes the winner undefined - and the losing case is fail-open (a stale 'granted' row shadows a withdrawal). The FOR UPDATE lock at line 129 serialises withdrawals against each other but not against record_consent, which takes no lock.
findings.fix: Add a monotonic tiebreaker (a BIGSERIAL sequence column, or ORDER BY consented_at DESC, id DESC) used by both readers, use a DB-side timestamp default, and take the same users-row lock in record_consent.

findings.issue: POST /api/consent/withdraw is destructive (withdrawing data_processing deactivates the account and there is no re-grant path for it) but has no @limiter.limit and no step-up re-authentication, unlike the auth routes (app/routers/auth.py:30, :194). Refuted as a BLOCK: an attacker holding the session cookie can already call DELETE /api/applications/account with mode=hard_delete (pre-existing, strictly worse), so the new endpoint grants no additional capability, and SameSite=lax plus origin-restricted CORS prevent a cross-site trigger.
findings.fix: Apply a modest rate limit and require a fresh TOTP/password confirmation for scopes whose effect is irreversible (data_processing), ideally for DELETE /api/applications/account at the same time.

findings.issue: WithdrawConsentResponse.account_deletion is typed dict[str, Any] and returns execute_deletion's internal summary verbatim. Today soft_delete returns only mode/message/hard_delete_after (no PII), but the same function's other modes return schema_dropped (the tenant schema name) and removed/retained field lists, so any future change to the deletion summary leaks straight through the API with no schema review.
findings.fix: Declare an explicit AccountDeletionSummary model with the three soft-delete fields and map into it, so the response surface cannot widen implicitly.

findings.issue: The app installs only SessionMiddleware and CORSMiddleware - no Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options or X-Content-Type-Options - and CSRF protection for the new cookie-authenticated POST relies entirely on the access_token cookie being SameSite=lax (app/routers/auth.py:118). That is a real mitigation for cross-site POST, so no CSRF finding is raised, but it is the only layer; a future switch to SameSite=none or a token in a header would silently expose /api/consent/withdraw.
findings.fix: Add a security-headers middleware and, for state-changing routes, a double-submit CSRF token or an Origin/Sec-Fetch-Site check as defence in depth.

findings.issue: Acknowledged pre-existing gap, re-confirmed as now reachable from the new endpoint: _soft_delete only sets is_active=False and audits a 30-day deadline - it never writes users.scheduled_deletion_at and no job purges accounts afterwards. A user who withdraws data_processing is told 'Permanent deletion scheduled in 30 days' in the API response while nothing will actually erase the data. deletion.py is out of scope for this change (R12) and was correctly left untouched.
findings.fix: Out of scope here; track as a follow-up story - persist the deadline and add a purge task, or soften the response message so it does not promise a deletion that no job performs.

refuted_candidates: Missing/weak authz on GET /api/consent and POST /api/consent/withdraw - refuted: both depend on get_current_user (app/dependencies.py:11), which requires the access_token cookie, an existing active user and totp_verified; neither endpoint accepts a client-supplied user id, so there is no IDOR surface.

SQL/identifier injection via schema_name in consent_service.disable_auto_apply - refuted: get_tenant_db -> tenant_session -> validate_schema_name enforces ^u_[0-9a-f]{32}$ before any SET search_path (app/database.py:15).

IP/User-Agent leakage in responses or audit trail - refuted on the normal path: audit('consent.withdrawn') carries only user_id and scope names (consent_store.py:140), ConsentView/ConsentEntry expose event, flags and timestamp only, and the auto_apply logs carry user_id plus scope. Leakage exists only on the DB-error path, filed as SEC-004.

Fail-open consent gate - refuted: consent_allows returns False for a missing record and additionally requires consented_to_data_processing (consent_store.py:96); a DB failure in current_consent propagates and the Celery task retries rather than proceeding.

LLM processing after withdrawal - refuted for all executed paths: the only call sites that ship user data to a provider are resume_service.generate_tailored_resume (auto_apply.py:211) and cover_letter_service.generate_cover_letter (auto_apply.py:244), both inside the non-HITL branch behind the gate at line 96; the HITL branch queues and continues without any LLM call; naukri._answer_screening_questions is string matching against the profile, not an LLM; screening_service.answer_screening_question has no caller.

Race allowing a stale 'granted' flag to be copied back into a withdrawal row - refuted for concurrent withdrawals: withdraw_consent takes SELECT users.id ... FOR UPDATE (consent_store.py:129) in the same transaction before reading the latest record, so two concurrent withdrawals serialise. The unlocked grant path is filed as SEC-005.

Input validation on the withdraw body - refuted: WithdrawConsentRequest uses Literal scopes, min_length=1 and extra='forbid' (422), NoConsentOnRecord maps to 409, and consent_store._checked_scopes re-validates in the service layer.

CSRF on POST /api/consent/withdraw - refuted: the access_token cookie is HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite=lax, which is not sent on cross-site POST, and CORS allow_origins is limited to settings.frontend_url.

Hardcoded secrets / injection / unsafe deserialisation in the diff - none: no credentials, no raw SQL (migration 0006 is static DDL), no pickle/yaml, no dependency manifest changed (so no audit step was required).
